news.title: Democrats Lead Republicans in 5 States Trump Won by Double Digits: Map
news.text: Democrats are mounting competitive Senate and gubernatorial campaigns in several states that President Donald Trump carried by double-digit margins in the 2024 presidential election. The competitive contests in Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Ohio and Texas have raised questions about whether Republicans, who hold both the House and Senate majorities, face mounting political headwinds ahead of the 2026 midterms and whether Democrats can capitalize on them. Trump’s Slipping Approval Rating Costas Panagopoulos, a political science professor at Northeastern University, told Newsweek that "presidential approval and the state of the economy are both strong predictors to outcomes in congressional races in midterms. The president's sagging rating on both of these metrics are making races in these states more competitive than we'd expect.” Trump's approval ratings have raised concerns among some Republicans as the party heads into the 2026 midterms. Nationally, 35 percent of voters approve of Trump's job performance while 59 percent disapprove as of August 27, leaving him significantly underwater with a net approval rating of -24, according to Civiqs' rolling online tracking poll of registered voters. The survey has garnered 126,377 responses since January 20, 2025, when Trump was inaugurated for a second term. An August 25 Economist/YouGov poll found 35 percent of Americans approved of the president's job performance, with a net approval rating of -26. Compared to a similar poll during the same point in his first term, his net approval rating was -9 and former Democratic President Joe Biden’s -12. Aggregators like RealClearPolitics show Trump with a 40 percent approval rating and 57 percent disapproval, while the Silver Bulletin puts his approval rating at 38 percent. A new Strength in Numbers/Verasight poll fielded August 14-19, which surveyed 1,514 U.S. adults ages 18 and older, found Trump underwater on all 12 issues it tracks, as border security—his last positive rating—slipped to −5. The poll had a margin of sampling error of plus or minus 2.6 percent. Alex Patton, owner of strategic public affairs firm Ozean Media, told Newsweek via email that the current climate is not a result of just one factor; rather it is being driven by a “toxic soup of mega-trends of economic factors, inflation, gas prices, grocery prices, the job market, the President's record-low approval numbers (especially with Independents), the quagmire in Iran, and, in some cases, terrible candidates.” He described the current political environment as “terrible, gawd-awful” for the GOP, “with maybe the only win being the stock market, and the stock market is not the economy.” Hans Noel, a professor of government at Georgetown University, told Newsweek that “Trump has involved himself even more in the midterms, so voters are even less likely to not think of him when they vote.” Trump’s 2024 Election Victory Trump won the 2024 election against then-Vice President Kamala Harris, securing 312 Electoral College votes to Harris' 226 and winning the national popular vote. Trump carried 31 states overall, including 24 by double-digit margins, and clinched all the swing states. His margins among the states he won by double digits ranged from Ohio, which he won by 11.2 percentage points, to deeply Republican Wyoming, where he won by 45.8 points. Other states he won by double digits included Alaska, Florida, Iowa, Kansas, Ohio, South Carolina, Tennessee and West Virginia. Republicans also regained control of the Senate in 2024, flipping Democratic-held seats and securing a majority in the chamber, while maintaining control of the House of Representatives. At the state level, Republicans entered 2025 holding a majority of governorships nationwide. “At the end of the day, in 2024 Donald Trump was a rising tide lifting all Republican boats, but in 2026 he is a falling tide lowering all Republican boats from sea to shining sea," Mark Jones, a politics professor at Rice University, told Newsweek. 2026 Midterms Political experts note that losses by the party controlling the White House are common in midterm elections. However, they also caution against viewing the 2026 midterms solely as a referendum on Trump, noting that while the president's approval ratings and the national political environment are likely to play the largest role in the elections, factors such as candidate quality, local issues and state-specific dynamics are also helping shape a number of competitive races. “Democrats lost 63 House seats and six Senate seats in the 2010 midterm, then another 13 House seats and nine Senate seats in 2014, both under Obama,” Matt Klink, owner and president of Klink Campaigns, told Newsweek, noting that those elections occurred under presidents who were more popular than Trump is now. He added that Republicans also faced significant setbacks during Trump's first term, noting that “Republicans lost 40 House seats in 2018, Trump's own first midterm.” Many analysts suggest that Trump's standing with voters is giving Democrats opportunities in states that would normally be difficult targets. Doug Gordon, a Democratic strategist at Upshift Strategies, told Newsweek, “Trump's historic unpopularity and the fact that the majority of voters believe that he has failed to deliver on his promise to lower prices have given Democrats an excellent opportunity to compete in states that might have otherwise been out of reach,” while cautioning that there is still a long way to go before Election Day. Not all analysts view the races primarily through a national lens, though. Tim Hagle, an associate professor in the Department of Political Science at the University of Iowa, noted that “midterms also tend to be more about local issues,” though he said campaigns can sometimes become nationalized, a strategy he believes both parties are pursuing this cycle. Still, some observers say the Senate map looks markedly different from it did just a few months ago. Reflecting on the shifting landscape, Jones told Newsweek that “six months ago, the best Democrats looked likely to be able to achieve in the U.S. Senate was a reduction of the Republican advantage to 51-49 for the final two years of Donald Trump’s term in office, but today they have a clear pathway to a majority, one which only requires them to win three of the current six toss up races.” Noel from Georgetown University said, “In general, the Democratic Party has been trying to find a way to break through to voters they have lost to Trump, and midterm elections are great place to experiment with that.” Voters will determine the balance of power in Congress and a series of state races in less than 75 days. Alaska Trump easily carried Alaska in the 2024 presidential election, winning 54.5 percent of the vote to Harris' 41.4 percent, a margin of about 13.1 percentage points. Despite Alaska's Republican tilt at the presidential level, Democrats have remained competitive in statewide races, aided in part by the state's ranked-choice voting system. Alaska has voted Republican in every presidential election since 1968, with comfortable margins for Trump in the past three elections. The state has not elected a Democratic governor since Tony Knowles left office in 2002, and the state's last Democratic U.S. senator, Mark Begich, left office in 2015. Alaska Senate Race The Senate contest has emerged as one of Democrats' more plausible pickup opportunities in 2026. Republican Senator Dan Sullivan is seeking another term, while Democrats are backing former Representative Mary Peltola, who won a special House election in 2022 before losing reelection in 2024. Dave Hopkins, a political science professor at Boston College, told Newsweek, “Senate Democrats are benefiting from a successful recruiting year for Senate candidates, particularly in Alaska where Mary Peltola was the strongest possible Democratic nominee.” Polling shows a tight race. A Data for Progress survey of 605 likely voters in Alaska found that in the first round of voting, no candidate received an outright majority, with 47 percent saying they would vote for Peltola compared to 41 percent for Sullivan. In Alaska, all candidates appear on a single ballot regardless of party, and the four with the most support advance to the general election. Three percent said they would vote for Gerald Heikes, another Republican candidate, while 5 percent were undecided. In the final round of ranked-choice voting, however, Peltola led Sullivan by 6 points, 53 percent to 47 percent, according to the poll. It surveyed 605 likely voters in Alaska from July 28 to August 4, 2026 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 4 percentage points. An Alaska Survey Research poll put Peltola ahead of Sullivan 50.8 percent to 49.2 percent in the final round. It surveyed 1,371 likely voters from August 2-5, 2026, and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3 percentage points. However, a June New York Times/Siena College poll found Sullivan ahead 47 percent to 45 percent, with about 5 percent undecided. The poll of 593 Alaskan voters was conducted between June 15 and 19 and has a margin of error of plus or minus 4.9 percentage points. The Cook Political Report and Sabato’s Crystal Ball rate the race as a “toss up.” While Alaska's open governor's race is expected to be competitive, major election forecasters still give Republicans an edge. Ohio “Ohio is the one to watch,” Klink told Newsweek. Patton and Hagle also noted that the state represents Democrats' strongest pickup opportunity of the cycle. Trump carried the state by about 11 percentage points in 2024, an improvement over his 2020 and 2016 performances, when he won by about 8 points each time. But Ohio was viewed as more competitive for Democrats not long before. Former President Barack Obama narrowly carried Ohio in 2008 and 2012. It has shifted as Trump performed well among the state’s working-class voters. Despite that Republican trend, Ohio has a history of electing Democrats statewide. The state's most recent Democratic senator was Sherrod Brown, who served from 2007 until his defeat by Republican Bernie Moreno in 2024. Brown is now seeking a return to the Senate in a 2026 race against Republican Senator Jon Husted, who was appointed to fill the remainder of Vice President JD Vance's term. Ohio Senate Race Brown, who represented Ohio in the Senate for 18 years, is now facing Husted for the full-term Senate seat. An August Fox News poll found Brown leading Husted by 8 points, 53 percent to 45 percent, with about 2 percent undecided. Brown leads among independents in Ohio by 38 points, 66 percent to 28 percent for Husted. The poll of 1,008 registered Ohio voters was conducted August 6-10. A Wedgewood Poll of 800 likely voters conducted between August 11 and 13 found Brown with 48 percent to Husted’s 44 percent. About 8 percent of voters were undecided. The poll has a margin of error of plus or minus 4 percentage points. Forecasters like the Cook Political Report and Sabato’s Crystal Ball view the race as a toss-up. Sabato’s Crystal Ball shifted it from Lean Republican earlier in June after Brown and Husted formally won their parties’ nominations. Ohio Governor’s Race The state's most recent Democratic governor was Ted Strickland, who served from 2007 to 2011. Ohio has elected only Republican governors since then, including current Governor Mike DeWine, who won reelection in 2022 but is now term-limited. Democrat Amy Acton, the former director of the Ohio Department of Health who gained statewide prominence during the COVID-19 pandemic, is facing Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, a former presidential candidate and DOGE member. Polls point to a close matchup. The same Wedgewood poll found an even tighter race for the governor’s mansion, with Acton ahead by 1 point, 47 percent to Ramaswamy’s 46 percent. Seven percent of the participants were undecided. A Fox News poll conducted August 6 to 10 among 1,008 registered voters put Ramaswamy ahead, 50 percent to 48 percent. The survey has a margin of error of plus or minus 3 percentage points. Tulchin Research found Acton leading 46 percent to 44 percent in a survey sponsored by John Kulewicz, the Democratic candidate for Ohio attorney general. The survey, conducted July 29 to August 4 among 660 likely voters, had a margin of error of plus or minus 4 percentage points. A New York Times/Siena College poll of 601 likely voters, conducted June 15 to 28, had the candidates tied at 47 percent. Its margin of error was plus or minus 4.7 percentage points. An AARP survey conducted June 14 to 16 by Democratic firm Impact Research and Republican firm Fabrizio, Lee & Associates gave Acton a 47 percent to 44 percent lead among 800 likely voters. Its margin of error was plus or minus 3.5 percentage points. The Cook Political Report rates the race as a toss-up after moving it from the Lean Republican column in a July update. Explaining the shift, the forecaster wrote that “it’s an inescapable law of politics: Money can only propel a campaign so far when its candidate’s flaws act as an anchor.” Texas Texas has backed Republican presidential nominees in every election since 1980, but Democrats hope 2026 will offer one of their best opportunities in years to compete statewide. Trump carried Texas by 13.7 percentage points in 2024, defeating Harris 56 percent to around 42.5 percent. Texas has not elected a Democrat to statewide office since 1994, making it one of the nation's longest-running Republican strongholds. Democrats have repeatedly targeted the state as demographic shifts and population growth have reshaped its electorate, but they have fallen short in a series of closely watched campaigns, including Beto O'Rourke's 2018 Senate bid against Ted Cruz. Texas Senate Race The GOP's decades-long hold on Texas statewide offices will be tested in November, with the Senate race between Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton and Democratic state Representative James Talarico nearly deadlocked. Surveys show both Paxton, who is endorsed by Trump, and Talarico, who has served as a state representative since 2018, holding narrow leads at different points in the campaign. The matchup follows Paxton's defeat of longtime Senator John Cornyn in the Republican primary in late May. “Texas is the wild card: with Ken Paxton defeating John Cornyn in the GOP primary, Democrats inherited a nominee carrying real legal baggage. Right now, the race is less about James Talarico and more about Ken Paxton, his money problems, and his personal foibles,” Klink said. Jones also spoke about Paxton’s reputational and legal history to Newsweek, stating, “Candidate quality is an issue for Republicans in a few instances, and is having an especially negative impact on Republican prospects in Texas where Ken Paxton arguably is the weakest major statewide Republican candidate in modern Texas GOP history.” Hopkins said his “scandal-ridden past seems to be a serious liability.” In 2023, the Republican-controlled Texas House impeached Paxton on 20 articles. The Texas Senate acquitted him. Paxton has repeatedly dismissed the impeachment and other allegations as politically motivated. Accusations of bribery and infidelity also circulated during the impeachment trial, with one of the articles stating that Paxton “benefited from Nate Paul’s employment of a woman with whom Paxton was having an extramarital affair.” His wife, state Senator Angela Paxton, filed for divorce in 2025, following “recent discoveries” and citing “biblical grounds.” Polls appear to flip-flop on who is leading, as a recent Emerson College Polling/Nexstar Media poll of 1,000 likely Texas voters puts the Senate race in a near dead heat, with 47 percent backing Paxton and 46 percent supporting Talarico. About 5 percent are undecided and 2 percent back a different candidate. The poll was conducted August 9-11 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3 percentage points. A Fox News poll of 1,006 registered Texas voters found that 51 percent back Talarico and 48 percent Paxton, with 1 percent undecided. The survey was conducted July 23-27 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 4 percentage points. The Cook Political Report and Sabato’s Crystal Ball rate the race as “toss up.” Iowa Iowa was viewed as a battleground for much of the 2000s, with Obama carrying the state by about 10 points in 2008 and 6 points in 2012. But Trump performed well in the state in each of his presidential bids, winning by 10 points in 2016, 8 points in 2020 and 13 points in 2024. Iowa Senate Race Republican Representative Ashley Hinson is going against Democratic state Representative Josh Turek in the Iowa Senate race. They are running to succeed Republican Senator Joni Ernst, who chose not to run for reelection. Democrats haven't secured a Senate seat in the state since Tom Harkin's election in 2008. Turek is a two-time Paralympic gold medalist and state House member, first elected in 2022. Obama endorsed him in a late-July video, while Trump has endorsed Hinson, who was first elected in 2020 after serving in the state House and working as a journalist. “I'm not sure Iowa's Senate race is as close as some polls show, but we do have three competitive House races too, so Democrats are hopeful,” Hagle from the University of Iowa said. An Emerson poll this month found Hinson with a slight lead, 47.5 percent to 45 percent. She was viewed favorably by 44 percent of respondents and unfavorably by 40 percent, while Turek was viewed favorably by 42 percent and unfavorably by 27 percent. It surveyed 712 likely voters August 2-4 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.7 percentage points. A Fox News poll of 1,003 Iowa registered voters found Turek leading Hinson 50 percent to 46 percent, with 4 percent undecided. The poll was conducted June 23-27 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3 percentage points. The Cook Political Report updated the race's rating from leaning Republican to a toss-up on August 20. Sabato’s Crystal Ball rates the race as “leans Republican.” Polling averages suggest a competitive contest. RealClearPolling's average shows the race nearly tied, with Hinson at 47 percent and Turek at 46.3 percent. Iowa Governor’s Race Republican Governor Kim Reynolds, who has led the state since 2017, is not seeking reelection. The last time a Democrat won Iowa’s governorship was in 2006, when Chet Culver was elected. Culver lost his reelection in 2010 to Republican Terry Branstad, and Republicans have been in office ever since. Iowa State Auditor Rob Sand, a Democrat, is going up against Republican businessman Zach Lahn in the state's open governor's race. “For Republicans, Lahn is basically an unknown. His victory in the primary was a surprise, likely to him as well, and he's had to work on increasing his name ID,” Hagle told Newsweek, contrasting him with Sand’s name recognition given his state role. “Sand has built a brand as a ‘numbers-guy auditor’ that plays well with independents,” Klink added. A Suffolk University poll released Wednesday found Sand ahead of Lahn 48 percent to 44 percent among 500 likely Iowa voters, with 9 percent undecided. The survey, conducted August 20-23, has a margin of error of plus or minus 4.4 percentage points. Sand's advantage has held across a string of surveys this summer, though its size keeps shifting. An Emerson College Polling survey put Sand up to 48 percent, while Trump fell to 43 percent. Two percent of respondents said they would vote for someone else, while 7 percent were still undecided. The survey polled 712 likely voters August 2-4 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.7 percentage points. A survey from The New York Times and Siena University, conducted among 600 likely voters June 15-27, showed Sand up a single point, 48 percent to 47 percent. Meanwhile, a Fox News poll showed Sand up 9 points, 53 percent to 44 percent. Beach Research and Shaw & Company Research conducted it from June 23-27 among 1,003 registered voters. The Cook Political Report rates the race lean Democratic, while Sabato's Crystal Ball places it in the toss-up category. Kansas Kansas has been a reliable state for the Republican Party at the presidential level for decades. Trump carried Kansas by 16.2 percentage points in 2024, defeating Harris 56.2 percent to 40 percent. The state has not voted for a Democratic presidential nominee since Lyndon B. Johnson's landslide victory in 1964. Kansas’ Governor’s Race Kansas' open governor's race has emerged as one of Democrats' more surprising opportunities in 2026. Democrat Cindy Holscher is seeking to succeed term-limited Governor Laura Kelly, one of the few Democratic governors in a state Trump carried by double digits. Republicans have nominated Ty Masterson and are favored by most forecasters, with the Cook Political Report and Sabato’s Crystal Ball both rating the race as lean Republican. There hasn’t been much public polling of the general election, but early polls show a competitive race. A recent Global Strategy Group survey found Holscher leading Masterson by 1 percentage point, though the result was within the poll's margin of error of plus or minus 4 percentage points. The Democratic sponsored poll of 600 likely voters was conducted between August 13 and 16. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Jason Lemon and Sam Wilson.
news.summary: Democrats are making states Trump won by double-digit margins in 2024 competitive ahead of the 2026 midterms.
news.author: Mandy Taheri

news.title: Trump 'Skipping 25th Anniversary 9/11 Ceremony' in New York to Visit His Golf Course in Ireland
news.text:
Donald Trump is skipping the upcoming memorial commemoration in Manhattan for the 25th anniversary of the terrorist attack on the World Trade Center, RadarOnline.com has learned.

The president will instead mark the grim milestone in a much smaller way, before jetting off to his golf course in Ireland for the Irish Open.Donald Trump Will Not Speak at Manhattan MemorialTrump's decision to pass on the ceremony reportedly came after he was told he would not be able to speak at the hallowed site now known as ground zero. 

According to The New York Times, Trump had planned to attend, and staffers made advance visits to the site to prepare for his appearance. 

He also wanted to speak at the event. However, the National September 11 Memorial and Museum has prohibited politicians from delivering speeches at the annual commemoration since 2012 in an effort to keep the event nonpartisan and focused solely on victims and their families.

After learning he would not be allowed to speak, the 80-year-old canceled his plans, and will instead pay tribute at the Pentagon, site of the second terror attack on Sept. 11, 2001.

Vice President J.D. Vance is expected to represent the White House at the New York event. Former Presidents Bill Clinton, George W. Bush, and Barack Obama are also expected to attend, along with former New York City Mayor Rudy Giuliani.Donald Trump Set to Tee Off OverseasThe president's travel plans reportedly also played a part in the decision to avoid Manhattan. Trump is scheduled to depart for his golf course in Doonbeg, Ireland, the day after the anniversary. Leaving from Joint Base Andrews in Maryland would cause fewer disruptions than departing from New York or New Jersey. 

Trump last attended the ground zero ceremony in 2024, alongside then-President Joe Biden and then-Vice President Kamala Harris.

Anna Kelly, a White House spokeswoman, did not address the president's plans in response to The Times' request for comment.

"On the 25th anniversary of this tragic day, the president will remember those who were killed at the hands of evil terrorists, honor their loved ones, and pay tribute to the brave first responders who put their lives on the line to rescue their fellow Americans," she simply told the outlet.Donald Trump Claimed He 'Warned' Government About Osama Bin LadenTrump was engulfed in controversy after last year's ceremony, when he bizarrely claimed he warned the government about Osama Bin Laden a full year before the terror attacks.

While addressing a crowd of sailors and officers at the U.S. Navy's 250th anniversary celebration in Norfolk, Virginia, Trump highlighted the force's accomplishments before telling the audience he "had to take a little credit" for sounding an alarm about the Al-Qaeda chief more than a decade before his death.

Trump said: "And please remember I wrote about Osama bin Laden exactly one year ago, one year before he blew up the World Trade Center." 

He later added: "I said, 'You got to watch Osama bin Laden.' And the fake news would never let me get away with that statement unless it was true."Donald Trump Takes CreditTrump appeared to be referring to his 2000 book, The America We Deserve, co-written with Dave Shiflett.

He continued: "But I can tell you there's a page in there devoted to the fact that I saw somebody named Osama bin Laden and I didn't like it, and you've gotta take care of him. They didn't do it. A year later, he blew up the World Trade Center."

"So, (I) gotta take a little credit because nobody else is going to give it to me. You know the old story: If they don't give you credit, just take it yourself."
news.summary: Trump's decision to pass on the ceremony reportedly came after he was told he would not be able to speak at the hallowed site.

news.title: Trump Backed Out of 9/11 25th Anniversary Ceremony Because Organizers Wouldn’t Allow Him to Give a Speech: Report
news.text:
NEED TO KNOW

President Donald Trump is reportedly skipping the New York City ceremony commemorating the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 terrorist attacksThe president will instead mark the anniversary at the Pentagon after officials at the New York memorial denied his request to make a speech, according to The New York TimesVice President JD Vance is expected to attend this year’s N.Y.C. ceremony in Trump’s place

President Donald Trump is reportedly skipping the New York City ceremony commemorating the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks after officials denied his request to make a speech, according to The New York Times.

Organizers at the National Sept. 11 Memorial and Museum have barred politicians from speaking since 2012, according to the Times and an Associated Press report from that time.

The White House did not acknowledge the Times’ reporting on the request to make a speech when reached for comment by PEOPLE on Friday, Aug. 28.

“As a proud New Yorker, President Trump has spoken about his own experiences watching the horrific events of September 11, 2001,” White House spokesperson Anna Kelly said in a statement. “On the 25th anniversary of this tragic day, the President will remember those who were killed at the hands of evil terrorists, honor their loved ones, and pay tribute to the brave first responders who put their lives on the line to rescue their fellow Americans.”

Instead of the Ground Zero ceremony, the longtime New Yorker will attend the annual commemoration at the Pentagon, as he did last year. During the 2024 election, Trump attended the New York ceremony alongside then-President Joe Biden and his campaign rival, Vice President Kamala Harris.

Vice President JD Vance is expected to attend this year’s ceremony in Manhattan, and administration officials will also be present at the Flight 93 Memorial outside Shanksville, Pa.

Former Presidents Bill Clinton, George W. Bush and Barack Obama are expected to attend the New York event at the site of the Twin Towers, as are former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, former first lady Laura Bush, and former New York City Mayor Rudy Giuliani, according to the Times.

Prior to the 25th anniversary of the deadliest attack on the United States since Pearl Harbor, Trump will be in Texas for a Republican convention ahead of November’s midterms. Then, on Sept. 12, he leaves for Ireland to attend the Irish Open at one of his golf courses.

Trump opened his remarks at the Pentagon in 2025 by memorializing Charlie Kirk, a longtime ally and political operative who was assassinated the day before during an event at a Utah college. He announced he planned to give Kirk the Presidential Medal of Freedom posthumously.

“This morning, we recall the light of America’s best and bravest and the love that they showed in their final moments,” Trump said of the emergency workers and everyday Americans who saved lives during the 2001 attacks. “We will honor always our great heroes, and you are our heroes. There’s a group of people that don’t want to talk about our heroes, but we will always talk about our heroes.”

Later that evening, he attended the New York Yankees game in the Bronx.

In 2012, Joe Daniels — the then-president of the 9/11 Memorial & Museum — told the AP that their decision to limit politicians’ remarks was intended to honor “the victims and their families in a way free of politics.”

Trump, who made his name and grew his businesses for decades in New York, was in the city when the Twin Towers were attacked on Sept. 11, 2001. He called into a New Jersey television station that day and claimed that one of his buildings would now be the tallest in lower Manhattan.

Trump’s building “actually was the second-tallest building in downtown Manhattan, and it was actually — before the World Trade Center — was the tallest,” the future president said at the time. “And then, when they built the World Trade Center, it became known as the second-tallest. And now it’s the tallest.”

“It’s just gone and it’s just hard to believe,” he added of the World Trade Center. “The big thing that you really will have to do is never forget. You just can’t forget that something like this happened.”

news.title: New Data Shows Gen Z Regrets Voting For Trump
news.text:
New data from public opinion research firm Navigator found that 31 percent of Generation Z said they regret voting for President Donald Trump in the 2024 election.

Generation Z showed more regret about their voting choices compared with 28 percent of Millennials, 20 percent of Generation X, and 10 percent of Baby Boomers, who all said they regretted voting for Trump, according to the data, compiled from several surveys taken between June 4 and July 27. Alternatively, 69 percent of Generation Z said they did not regret voting for Trump, compared with 72 percent of Millennials, 80 percent of Generation X, and 90 percent of Baby Boomers.

In addition, Trump has the lowest approval rating among Generation Z, with only 33 percent of voters saying they either strongly approve or somewhat approve of the way he is handling his job as president. Trump had a 38 percent approval rating among Millennials, 39 percent among Generation X, and 41 percent among Baby Boomers. (RELATED: Nearly One-Third Of Gen Z Steers Clear Of Car Insurance, Survey Finds)

Furthermore, Generation Z is the most pessimistic about the direction of the country, with a net of -42 saying the country is headed in the right direction compared with Millennials (net -35), Generation X (net - 34), and Baby Boomers (net -27), the same data shows. Fifty percent of voters between the ages of 18-44 said they disapproved of Trump’s handling of the economy but also do not trust Democrats on the issue.

Notably, Trump’s war against Iran continues to be deeply unpopular, with 52 percent of respondents saying they either strongly or somewhat oppose the military action.

Gen Z regrets Trump support and is midterm motivatedhttps://t.co/GTdzo9y48M— The Hill (@thehill) August 28, 2026

Tina Tang, director of polling and analytics at Navigator, discussed the data with The Hill.

“Young Americans are telling us that politics is deeply important to who they are, but it doesn’t mean they’re happy with the current political system, or that they’re even optimistic about the direction of the country as a whole,” Tang said.

“Young Americans are disproportionately represented among people who are dissatisfied with Trump and the economy. It doesn’t mean they’re flocking to one party or another.”

“Gen Z is not a group that’s hard to understand. Politics are important to them, but they are also pessimistic about the economy right now,” she continued.

Navigator identified Generation Z voters as individuals who were born between 1998 and 2008.

Data from the Pew Research Center shows Trump received 45 percent of the vote among individuals between 18 and 49 in 2024, compared to former Vice President Kamala Harris, who received 52 percent of the vote among the same age group.

The Navigator data was compiled from several polls conducted between June 4 and July 27.
news.summary: 31 percent said they regretted voting for the president

news.title: Richest Man in the World Currently Ranks 4th in Race to Bribe the Most Politicians

Elon Musk currently ranks fourth in a new list of the biggest political donors in the lead up to the midterm elections, according to an analysis by the New York Times. But the wealthiest man in the world is reportedly meeting with Speaker of the House Mike Johnson on Friday and there’s plenty of time for Musk to spread even more of his money around to support Republicans and President Donald Trump.

The New York Times looked at the 20 biggest donors, who have poured a combined $1.2 billion into candidates for federal elections this cycle. The top five include Marc Andreesen and Ben Horowitz ($115 million), George and Alex Soros ($103 million), Jeff Yass ($94 million), Elon Musk ($90 million), and the Republican nonprofit One Nation ($76 million), an arm of the Senate Leadership Fund. All donors in the top five except for the Soros family are supporting Republicans.

The tech oligarch was rewarded with the so-called Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), a conspiracy to decimate the federal government. Musk has authorized his super PAC, America PAC, to spend at least $100 million, but other reports have suggested he plans to spend as much as $200 million before the midterms are held in November. news.title: Why some Democrats running in red states are pushing away Biden, Harris
news.text:
With less than 70 days until the midterm election, some Democrats running in the most conservative areas are sending a clear message to former President Joe Biden and former Vice President Kamala Harris: stay out of their races.

In Iowa, Democratic Senate nominee state Rep. Josh Turek -- who has welcomed the support of former President Barack Obama and has twice won a seat in a district that voted for President Donald Trump -- was asked if Harris should campaign for him. He simply said "No."

Also in Iowa, Democratic gubernatorial nominee Rob Sand told Politico "no thanks" to the idea of Biden or Harris campaigning for him. He also said Harris should not run for president in 2028, arguing the country needs "new leadership."

Alaska Democratic Senate nominee Mary Peltola recently distanced herself from Harris after her political action committee backed Peltola in a fundraising email.

"Mary isn't seeking endorsements from anyone from the Lower 48 -- her focus is and always will be Alaska," Peltola's campaign told The New York Times.

The blunt rejections, coming within days of each other in two states Trump carried by double digits in 2024, underscore a reality for Democrats: candidates fighting for independent and moderate Republican voters increasingly see the party's brand and most recent presidential ticket as a liability.

The Senate races are particularly vital to Democrats, who are looking take control in the chamber where the GOP has a slim majority.

Putting 2024 in the rearview

Democratic strategist James Carville told ABC News that the Democratic Party is "just ready to move on from 2024" as "everybody’s scarred by it." He added that this phenomenon is not necessarily new, saying that "no Republicans" were looking for Mitt Romney's support in 2014 -- two years after Romney lost the 2012 election to Obama.

Carville added that Biden's prostate cancer diagnosis could be a limiting factor for his campaigning, and that "Democrats like Harris fine. They just don't find her particularly inspirational."

After the start of the Iraq War, when President George W. Bush's favorability ratings were down, he stuck to events with minimal press coverage in areas that were Republican strongholds, according to news reports at the time during the 2005-2006 midterm cycle.

During the run-up to the 2008 election, he barely appeared alongside John McCain, mostly holding private fundraisers out of the public eye.

Ashley Etienne, Harris' former communications director, said voters are disillusioned with the political establishment as "the Democratic Party's brand is in the tank."

Democratic strategist Matt Corridoni of the political organization, The Bench, which backs Peltola and Turek, said the candidates are signaling a break from the status quo.

"It doesn’t really make sense to have someone who was our nominee last cycle be on the trail for you," Corridoni said. "That represents the past. It represents partisan institutions."

A longtime Democratic donor who raised money for Harris' 2020 presidential campaign and asked not to be identified told ABC News, "Kamala showing up in Pennsylvania -- or Alaska, or Iowa -- she's not going to get the same enthusiasm as when she walks into South Carolina or New York City."

The donor added that Democrats need middle America appeal, "and you don't get the middle with Kamala."

The Harris team declined to comment on the recent remarks by Sand, Turek and Peltola. ABC News reached out to Biden's team for comment, but didn't hear back by the time of publication.

The politicalcalculus varies by district

Some say it all depends on the voters a candidate is trying to reach.

"Somebody like Mary Peltola who has a very good chance of flipping the Alaska Senate seat has to be very careful and strategic … that means ensuring she’s not bringing surrogates into the state or using their voices online in ways that could potentially turn off some of her very persuadable voters," said Adrienne Elrod, who served as Harris' senior adviser and spokesperson in 2024.

"There are some places where [Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez] is in demand, and there are some places where she's not. A lot of it just depends on the makeup of the target demographic that you're going for," Elrod added.

Some Democrats have actively sought Biden and Harris' support.

Former Biden White House aide Dan Koh, who is running to replace Rep. Seth Moulton in Massachusetts, told ABC News he asked Biden and Harris to endorse him. He said voters have told him they would vote for him because he has been backed by Biden.

"I've seen their integrity firsthand … I do not believe in running away from people that I believe in, that I've worked with," Koh said. "And I'm fortunate that the electorate has agreed."

Chris Jones, who's running to replace Republican incumbent French Hill in Arkansas, recently received Harris' endorsement, along with the support of Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg.

Asked whether Harris' backing is helpful in his red district and about Sand and Turek's remarks, Jones told ABC News, "campaigning is hard … every candidate is different, every constituency is different, and every moment is different."

Implications for 2028

The Harris donor said that if Turek, Sand or Peltola win in November, it could encourage other potential 2028 presidential contenders to further distance themselves from Harris and move more toward the center.

Red and purple state Democrats such as Beshear, Sen. Mark Kelly of Arizona and Buttigieg of Indiana -- all potential 2028 presidential contenders -- have recently campaigned in Iowa, showing an effort to reach voters well beyond the Democratic base. Beshear has campaigned for Sand; Kelly has campaigned for Turek and Buttigieg has campaigned for both Turek and Sand.

"If any one of them win," the donor said of Turek, Sand and Peltola, "you will see the [Pennsylvania Gov. Josh] Shapiros and the Beshears … maybe you'll have a Mark Kelly who will even move a little bit more center where they're going to say, 'look, we can't win this election by just winning blue states, we need to win purple states.'"

news.title: Longtime GOP Staffers Abandon Republicans to Work for Democrats
news.text: Republican staffers are abandoning the GOP to work for Democratic candidates in two Senate races Democrats hope to flip in the 2026 midterms. Democrats are hoping to expand the Senate battleground into more conservative states that backed President Donald Trump by double digits in the 2024 election, as his approval rating has fallen nationwide amid economic concerns and the unpopular war in Iran. The Democrats have little choice but to target these more difficult states, as the path to a Senate majority requires them to win traditionally Republican places like Texas. In Kansas, Democratic Senate candidate Adam Hamilton has hired Austin Gilpin, who has previously worked for Republicans in the Sunflower State. In Texas, Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico has announced that his campaign hired Jacob Smith, who worked for Republican Senator John Cornyn. The incumbent senator lost to conservative Attorney General Ken Paxton in the primary this year. Both are races Democrats hope to make competitive. In Texas, the race between Talarico and Paxton has become a toss-up despite the state backing Trump by 14 points in 2024. Republican Senator Roger Marshall is viewed as the favorite to win reelection in Kansas, but Democrats are hopeful about making the race competitive after fielding Hamilton, a pastor viewed as a viable candidate in the state that voted for Trump by 16 points in 2024. Hamilton, Talarico Hire GOP Staffers Hamilton hired Gilpin back in June, the campaign confirmed to Newsweek on Friday. The race is classified as Likely Republican by the Cook Political Report, as the state has historically leaned toward Republicans, though margins have narrowed in recent election cycles. Gilpin previously worked for the Kansas Republican Party, GOP Representative Ron Estes, and America Rising, according to his LinkedIn profile. He also worked on former GOP Governor Sam Brownback’s 2014 campaign, his LinkedIn shows. In a statement provided to Newsweek, Gilpin said Marshall “chose his party and his president over Kansas, and over decency.” “I didn't leave my values behind when I joined Adam's campaign. Republicans always have a seat at his table, and he is earning their support the same way he earned mine,” he said. “Our politics are fundamentally broken, and the chaos in Washington isn't working for anyone. We need leaders who are willing to find common ground, push back on the extremes, and get serious about solving real problems. Kansans of every party can trust Adam to fight for them.” Meanwhile, Smith is serving as Talarico’s deputy policy director after spending five years working for Cornyn as a deputy legislative director and policy adviser. Smith previously told Newsweek after his hiring was announced that Talarico “speaks to the needs of everyday people who day in and day out work too hard for too little.” “Ken Paxton is the most corrupt, self-dealing politician in Texas who would sell their futures to the highest contributor just to hold onto power. I’m encouraging all my fellow Republicans who know Ken Paxton is unfit to serve in the Senate to finally hold him accountable at the ballot box,” Smith said. Newsweek reached out to the Marshall, Paxton and Talarico campaigns for comment via email. Trump’s GOP Leaves Out Some Republicans Trump has reshaped the modern Republican Party in his brand of politics over the past decades. He remains overwhelmingly popular with the party’s conservative base that propelled him to the White House in both 2016 and 2024. But not everyone in the GOP has been on board with the rise of Trumpism. Some more traditional Republicans have found themselves alienated from the party. Some prominent Republicans disaffected with Trumpism, such as former Wyoming GOP Representative Liz Cheney, endorsed former Vice President Kamala Harris over Trump in the 2024 election. Can Adam Hamilton and James Talarico Win in Kansas and Texas? What Polls Show Both states backed Trump by double digits in the 2024 election, so they would not ordinarily be viewed as top targets for Democrats. But the party has few obvious pickup opportunities, with Maine and North Carolina being the most competitive, so they are eyeing these for potential upsets. Texas especially has emerged as a Senate battleground this year as polls show Talarico building up a polling lead over Paxton in the traditionally Republican state. Two new polls this week gave Talarico an advantage over Paxton. A new survey from Texas Public Opinion Research (TPOR) showed Talarico leading by 6 points, 48 percent to 42 percent. Meanwhile, a University of Texas/Texas Politics Project survey released earlier this week showed Talarico up 3 points over Paxton, 42 percent to 39 percent. The TPOR poll surveyed 1,000 likely voters from August 21 to 24, 2026 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.3 percentage points. The University of Texas poll surveyed 1,200 registered voters from August 5 to 13, 2026 and had a margin of error of ±3.58 percentage points. Polling on the Kansas race is more limited, with only Democratic internals being released over the past few months. A Public Policy Polling survey, sponsored by the Democratic-aligned Senate Majority PAC, showed Marshall up one point over Hamilton, 46 percent to 45 percent. A GBAO poll, sponsored by Hamilton, showed Marshall up 4 points, 47 percent to 43 percent. The Public Policy Polling survey was conducted among 569 voters from August 7 to 8, 2026, while the GBAO poll was conducted among 600 likely voters from July 8 to 13, 2026. Democratic Defections in Michigan While Republicans are dealing with defections in some races, Democrats are facing a similar issue in Michigan, where some moderate Democrats are vowing not to support the party’s nominee Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive. Critics have pointed to his positioning on Israel and health care as reasons they would vote for Republican Mike Rogers. El-Sayed has also faced criticism for his ties with Hasan Piker, a streamer and progressive activist. Michigan state Representative Karen Whitsett attended an event as part of a “Democrats for Rogers” coalition earlier in August. According to Michigan Advance, she said during the event that health care is a key issue for her driving her support for Rogers, as El-Sayed has been a supporter of Medicare for All. “You will lose your health insurance if the other candidate gets in office. There’s no ifs, ands, or buts about it. That is what Medicare for All means,” she said, according to the report. Representative Josh Gottheimer, a New Jersey Democrat, told CNN there is “no way I’m ever coming out for El-Sayed, right now.” Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Jason Lemon and Gray R. Thomas
news.summary: Democrats James Talarico and Adam Hamilton have both hired Republican staffers in their bids to win GOP-held Senate seats.

news.text:
Trump allies allege foreign interference as a host at an Israeli-funded media outlet has set its sights on targeting Vice President JD Vance.

The subject of the Trump-world ire is specifically commentary pushed by Emily Schrader, a media personality with the Jerusalem News Syndicate (JNS), a pro-Israel news and commentary outlet whose coverage generally reflects a conservative, right-leaning perspective. Schrader hosts JNS’s Axis of Truth podcast and co-hosts The Quad, a JNS YouTube show. Notably, JNS serves as a quasi-wire service for numerous Jewish-oriented publications across the U.S. (RELATED: Israel Could Be Propagandizing Christians At A Church Near You. Here’s How)

Since at least 2025, Schrader has used both her social media platforms and JNS to push unsubstantiated claims against the vice president. As well as level personal insults. 

In a post on X earlier this summer, Schrader referred to Vance as a “clown,” and in another made the outlandish suggestion that the vice president “wants the [Iranian] regime to survive lol.”

Schrader, in a July X post, appears to mock the idea that an “Israeli conspiracy” could be amplifying criticism of Vance, claiming instead that “national security experts have watched him misread the regime, smear allies, ignore Qatar’s documented influence operations, and now even portray 94 million Iranians as a terrorist threat.” Despite brushing aside allegations of a foreign-sourced effort to smear the vice president, Schrader is very open about her own foreign interests, describing herself on her personal website as an “American-Israeli journalist, author, and human rights activist” focused on Israeli and Iranian affairs.

Importantly, JNS, which hosts much of Schrader’s content, has received significant funding from the Adelson Family Foundation, according to a Jewish Telegraphic Agency report. More recently, Inside Philanthropy listed JNS among the foundation’s recent Israel advocacy grantees.

Aside from JNS, Schrader also appears frequently as a host on ILTV Israel News, which bills itself as “an independent English-language media company based in Tel Aviv, Israel that provides daily Israel news and entertainment to its viewers,” and “Israel’s Largest English News Channel.” ILTV was owned by Simon Falic — a close friend and ally of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu — and David Herzog up until May 2026, when it was sold to New York tech entrepreneur Reuven Moskowitz and the network’s CEO, Tom Zadok.

Despite numerous concerning connections to foreign interests — not least some running to the very top of the Israeli government — the same charge is a favorite of Schrader. In a video posted to her YouTube channel, Schrader similarly accused Donald Trump Jr. of doing business with individuals who have “concerning ties to Qatar” while alleging that he was selling access to the West Wing.

Schrader and JNS’s foreign ties have drawn scrutiny from a former Trump administration official, who told the Caller, “Textbook foreign interference. Schrader’s broader social media history also raises questions about her political positioning. Posts obtained by the Caller dating from 2020 through 2026 show her repeatedly criticizing Trump and aspects of his foreign policy.

In one post, she argued that a deal Trump was considering with the Islamic Republic would be worse for the region and the world than former President Barack Obama’s Iran nuclear agreement and could define his legacy as one of weakness and failure.

news.title: Trump to skip 9/11 remembrance at Ground Zero because they wouldn’t let him give a speech
news.text:
President Donald Trump reportedly plans to mark the 25th anniversary of the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks at the Pentagon, not Ground Zero in New York City – in part because he cannot give a speech. 

The president had initially intended to join former presidents and other officials in Manhattan on September 11, but those plans were changed after memorial planners seemingly reminded Trump’s team that politicians are barred from speaking at the site to maintain its nonpartisan stance, the New York Times reported.

Instead, Vice President JD Vance will represent the White House in New York City while Trump goes to the Pentagon, which also came under attack on September 11, 2001.

White House Spokesperson Anna Kelly said in a statement: “On the 25th anniversary of this tragic day, the President will remember those who were killed at the hands of evil terrorists, honor their loved ones, and pay tribute to the brave first responders who put their lives on the line to rescue their fellow Americans.” 

She added, “As a proud New Yorker, President Trump has spoken about his own experiences watching the horrific events of September 11, 2001.”

The president and First Lady Melania Trump also marked the September 11th anniversary at the Pentagon last year. At the memorial, Trump spoke about those who lost loved ones on September 11, 2001, while peppering in brags about his administration and agenda. 

“In America we take blows, but we never buckle. We bleed, but we do not bow, and we defy the fear, endure the flames and emerge from the crucible of every hardship stronger, prouder and greater than ever before,” Trump said during remarks last year.

The president then added: “Last year we were a dead country, now we have the hottest country anywhere in the world” – a statement he repeatedly shared during rallies and press conferences. 

Later that day, Trump flew to New York City to attend a New York Yankees game.

Since 2012, the National September 11 Memorial and Museum has prohibited politicians from speaking at Ground Zero – the site of the Twin Towers.

That decision was made after a series of political battles over the construction of the memorial site angered families who felt the political issues were overshadowing the memory of those who died that day. 

The last time Trump attended a 9/11 memorial in New York City was during the 2024 presidential race when he joined then-president Joe Biden, then-vice president Kamala Harris and other officials at Ground Zero. 

The politicians shook hands and stood side-by-side as they remembered the nearly 3,000 people who lost their lives as a result of the terrorist attack. 

This year, several notable politicians are expected to attend the 25th anniversary at Ground Zero, including former Mayor Rudy Giuliani; former President Bill Clinton and his wife, Hillary Clinton; former President George W. Bush and his wife, Laura Bush; and former President Barack Obama, officials familiar with the planning told the New York Times.

There are other reasons the president will mark the day from Washington, D.C., instead of New York City. 

The president is planning to travel to his golf course in Doonbeg, Ireland, the following day and it’s easier to leave from Joint Base Andrews in Maryland than the tri-state area airports, the New York Times reported.
news.summary: The 9/11 Memorial and Museum in New York City does not allow politicians to speak at Ground Zero to maintain a nonpartisan stance

news.title: Trump Snubs Ground Zero 9/11 Ceremony After Reportedly Being Denied Chance To Address Crowd
news.text: Donald Trump will stay away from this year's 25th anniversary ceremony at New York's 9/11 memorial after being told he would not be allowed to address mourners at Ground Zero, reports said.The National September 11 Memorial & Museum has barred speeches by elected officials at its annual commemoration since 2012, a policy intended to keep the event 'free of politics' and centred on victims' families. Politicians may attend, but they do not take the microphone.The New York Times reported that Trump's team had carried out advance visits to the Manhattan site, and that his interest in speaking from the Ground Zero podium had been relayed to event organisers in recent weeks.Sources as quoted by NYT said the request ran up against rules that have shaped the tightly choreographed ceremony for more than a decade, in which relatives read victims' names and officials stand in the audience rather than at a lectern.Trump To Mark 9/11 at the PentagonAccording to people familiar with internal White House discussions, Trump, 80, will instead mark the anniversary at the Pentagon, one of the other sites targeted on 11 September 2001. The attacks killed 2,996 people, including the 19 hijackers, across New York, Washington and near Shanksville, Pennsylvania, where United Airlines Flight 93 crashed.The president is expected to travel to Washington after attending a Republican midterms convention in Dallas on 9 and 10 September. The Times said officials may also work a tribute to 9/11 victims into the Dallas event, a prospect likely to draw scrutiny over the blending of commemoration with campaigning.Vice-President JD Vance is expected to represent the administration in New York instead. This year's ceremony will include six moments of silence, marking the times both World Trade Centre towers were struck and collapsed, the Pentagon attack and the crash of Flight 93, alongside the traditional reading of victims' names by family members.Trump last attended the Ground Zero ceremony in 2024 alongside then-President Joe Biden, then-Vice President Kamala Harris and Vance. No formal speeches were delivered on that occasion, in keeping with the memorial's rules.Memorial Stresses Presidents 'Always Welcome'The 9/11 Memorial & Museum did not comment directly on Trump's change of plans, but told the New York Post that presidents of both parties remained welcome at the site.'For more than a decade, the ceremony at Ground Zero has featured only family members solemnly reading the names of their loved ones,' it said, adding that elected officials had 'borne witness' to the occasion over the years and that 'every living President, including President Trump, has attended'.Travel arrangements may also be a factor. Trump is due to fly to his golf resort in Doonbeg, Ireland, on 12 September for the Irish Open, which runs from 10 to 13 September. The Times noted that departing from Joint Base Andrews in Maryland, rather than the New York area, would make the transatlantic journey more straightforward. The White House and the 9/11 Memorial & Museum were contacted for comment.The development adds to Trump's long-running and disputed commentary on 9/11. In March, he repeated a claim that he had 'predicted' Osama bin Laden would attack the World Trade Centre and had urged action against him a year before the attacks. A CNN fact-check of his 2000 book found only a single reference to bin Laden, with no warning of an imminent strike.

news.title: Democrats Try to Brush Aside 'Woke 1
news.text:
"'Woke 1' was crazy." So said Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) on ABC News' "This Week" earlier this month. 

She said she was quoting New York City Councilman Chi Osse, whom The New York Times characterizes as "far left." This was where Ocasio-Cortez seemed to be located on the ideological spectrum after her surprise defeat of House Democratic leadership member Joseph Crowley in the 2018 Democratic primary.

At that time, she was a 28-year-old former waitress and organizer for Sen. Bernie Sanders' (I-Vt.) 2016 presidential campaign. Today, a decade later, she's a nationally known figure often mentioned as a presidential candidate. In polls for the 2028 nomination, she ranks fourth in the RealClearPolitics average, behind 2024 nominee and former Vice President Kamala Harris, Gov. Gavin Newsom (D-Calif.) and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, and Polymarket places that her odds at winning are better than any of theirs.

As a possible national candidate, Ocasio-Cortez obviously has a motive to brush aside, as she did with a charmingly self-deprecatory laugh, the exotic positions she and other Democrats took on issues, particularly after the death of George Floyd in May 2020 and the ensuing multicity violent rioting.

They included demands to "defund the police" or even abolish police departments, to step up the already institutionalized demands for "diversity, equity and inclusion" hiring, and promotions in bureaucracies, public and private, for racial reparations. These weren't just words: Cities such as New York, San Francisco, Chicago and Minneapolis did hustle to partially defund their police departments.

The Floyd riots and calls for defunding police were immediately followed by a sharp spike upward in violent crime. Liberals have characterized that spike as a response to COVID-19, but charts compiled by writer Steve Sailer make it clear that the spike began not with the lockdowns but with the riots and Woke 1 depolicing.

At the same time, the lockdowns, enforced with Woke 1 censoriousness, were causing not just economic damage but also long-lasting harm to children who were kept out of teacher union-run schools long after it was clear children were not vectors of the virus. And Woke 1 transgender demands, for biological men on women's sports teams and public financing of even pre-adults' gender transition surgery, were advanced by the Biden administration and endorsed by Harris.

Now there are numerous signs that the nation is putting Woke 1 so far in the rearview mirror as to be invisible and has little appetite for Woke 2. Items include:

-- The lack of visible vehement protests at the elimination of DEI programs, racial quotas and preferences, in federal regulations, in many state and local governments, and even in their strongholds in the universities. You hear grumbling about the Supreme Court's 2023 ruling in Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard, but nothing like the politically charged attacks on its 2022 overturning of Roe v. Wade. There's covert opposition and attempts to retain DEI under different labels, but you don't hear Democratic candidates talking about the issue.

-- Similarly, there's a dog-who-didn't-bark response to the Trump administration's effective shutdown of illegal immigration on the southern border. Missing from the political dialogue have been media stories about the asylum-seekers who are obliged now to pursue their claims not from somewhere in the continental United States but from a not particularly helpful or sympathetic Mexico or somewhere even more distant.

-- Violent crime rates seem sharply down. After the Floyd riots, homicides rose even more in 2021 and seemed on a trajectory to reverse all the enormous progress in crime reduction accomplished since the reforms pioneered by former Mayor Rudy Giuliani in New York in the 1990s. Homicides declined in 2025 to below the lowest numbers of the post-Giuliani years, and the FBI reported that violent crime dropped 9.3%, the biggest drop since 1936. For 2026, statistics aren't fully available, but there are starkly lower rates of violent crime in New York, and Baltimore has seen a huge drop in homicides in the 2020s. Why the huge drop in violent crime? No one is sure, but it comes as Democratic politicians are hastening to assure us that they never actually really wanted to abolish the police and the prisons when they were saying so back in Woke 1.

-- The revelations of the hypocrisy and lies of Dr. Anthony Fauci and other public health officials during the COVID-19 epidemic. Fauci, who delighted in partying with Washington elites, according to his diaries, had to sit mute and invoke the Fifth Amendment as he was attacked credibly for having misled the public. Masking, he admitted privately, didn't prevent disease spread, even while he urged penalties for non-maskers. The vaccine, while reducing deaths, did not prevent transmission, as he had assured the nation. Fauci's efforts to discredit as "a conspiracy theory" the argument that the virus spread from a leak from the Wuhan laboratory he financed increasingly look very much like an effort to cover up the evidence that he financed the lab's gain-of-function research surreptitiously, to make the virus more dangerous, in violation of a presidential order. The initial order, by the way, came from former President Barack Obama, not President Donald Trump.

Against this evidence of the discrediting of Woke 1 come recent victories and near victories of members of or sympathizers with the Democratic Socialists of America, whose platform calls for the abolition of police and prisons. Those candidates have been emphasizing economic issues, however, which pass muster in Democratic primaries but may not in general electorates in states such as Michigan.

What is not apparent in the political landscape is nostalgia for Woke 1 police defunding, for heavy-handed statism like Fauci's COVID-19 regime, or for a revival of the Biden administration's open-borders immigration policy. Democrats may be able to capitalize on the current Trump slump this year. But for 2028, they may not be able to dismiss questions about Woke 1, and Woke 2, as flippantly as Ocasio-Cortez tried to do this month.

news.title: Why We Shouldn't Cancel the Supreme Court
news.text:
The following is adapted from a speech delivered on August 6, 2026, in Washington, D.C., at Hillsdale College’s Allan P. Kirby, Jr. Center for Constitutional Studies and Citizenship.

By Jonathan TurleyAuthor, Rage and the Republic: The Unfinished Story of the American Revolution

Nothing quite says popular justice like a good old-fashioned guillotine. Across the country, protesters have dragged around makeshift guillotines as they call for “radical” and “revolutionary” changes to our constitutional system. The symbol of the French Revolution remains a chilling reminder of how revolutions devour their own. What is even more unnerving than these prop guillotines is the increase in calls for radical and revolutionary changes — including the elimination or the packing of the Supreme Court, trashing the Electoral College, and doing away with the U.S. Senate — by establishment figures on the Left.

Today’s attacks on the American judiciary do indeed harken back to the rhetoric that raged before the advent of “The Terror” in revolutionary France — the rhetoric that gave rise to the kind of “mobocracy” that the Founders sought to avoid by designing our constitutional order as they did.

To help understand this, it is useful to recall the fundamental differences between the American Revolution, which led to the world’s oldest and most prosperous republic, and the French Revolution, which led to a short-lived, blood-soaked tyranny. Both revolutions were based on Enlightenment ideas. But America’s revolution was closely tied to the political philosophy of John Locke, who held that our rights come not from the government, but from God. The institutional arrangements of the Constitution, including the independent court system, were designed to protect these God-given individual rights.

Conversely, the French Revolution was inspired in the end not by Lockean principles but by the political philosophy of Jean-Jacques Rosseau, which extolled the “general will” of the people and opposed institutions (including courts) that interfered with that will. This concept of a general or popular will served as a license for French revolutionaries like Robespierre — who declared that “Terror is only justice: prompt, severe and inflexible . . . a natural consequence of the general principle of democracy” — to unleash a torrent of executions that would eventually come to turn on the revolutionaries themselves.

There is a radical movement rising in the U.S. with chilling parallels to the French Revolution. Demands for the elimination or packing of the Supreme Court and other measures are ripped from the French revolutionary handbook. Most worrisome is the surrender of establishment figures, particularly in promising to make radical changes to the Supreme Court. Indeed, offering the Supreme Court up to this movement has become a litmus test for Democratic presidential candidates. Former Vice President Kamala Harris, former Secretary of Transportation Pete Buttigieg, and U.S. Representative Ro Khanna have embraced it. Harris and California Governor Gavin Newsom have characterized reluctance to change the Court as “nostalgia” and have warned that “nostalgia is not working.” The platform of the increasingly influential Democratic Socialists of America calls both for dissolving the Supreme Court and for creating a unicameral legislature by eliminating the U.S. Senate.

Much of this is animated by undisguised power politics. Here’s former Attorney General Eric Holder arguing that packing the Supreme Court should be made a priority: “[We’re] talking about the acquisition and the use of power if there is a Democratic trifecta in 2028.” And Democratic strategist James Carville: “If the Democrats win the presidency and both houses of Congress, I think on day one, they should expand the Supreme Court to 13. . . . Eat our dust. Don’t run on it. Don’t talk about it. Just do it.” Harvard Law School Professor Michael Klarman has laid out an agenda by which the Democrats can guarantee that they will never lose another election but warns that “the Supreme Court could strike down everything [that agenda consists of].”

Massachusetts Senator Elizabeth Warren has characterized the Court as illegitimate because it has rendered decisions against what she sees as “widely held public opinion.” Former U.S. Representative Eric Swalwell similarly objected that the Court “defies the will of the people.” U.S. Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, who is now leading in some Democratic presidential polls, asks why we even have a Supreme Court: “How much does the current structure benefit us? . . . I don’t think it does.”

The irony is that those calling to pack the Court say it will make the Court “less partisan.” Buttigieg has suggested not only expanding the Court from nine to 15 justices, but also having each party appoint five members, with those ten justices then selecting the remaining five. Such a court would then operate like the Federal Election Commission currently does, with party loyalists voting the party line.

This way of thinking runs completely counter to our nation’s founding principles. A non-partisan, independent judiciary serves two essential purposes: it plays a vital role in preserving the separation of powers, which prevents all government power from being concentrated in one place, and it stands as a bulwark in defense of minority rights against a majority faction. To ensure its ability to perform these essential roles without being threatened by the political branches — the Congress and the executive branch — the Constitution gives federal jurists life tenure and salary protections.

Despite these structural protections, early in our nation’s history there were few professional standards governing the American court system. Courts were openly biased, with Federalist judges becoming virtual grand inquisitors of Jeffersonians under the infamous Alien and Sedition Acts passed during the presidency of John Adams. Judges and justices routinely ran for political office and openly engaged in political commentary from the bench. But this would change. The first university-based law school in the U.S. was founded in 1779 at The College of William & Mary in Williamsburg, Virginia, and America’s first independent law school was created in 1784 in Litchfield, Connecticut. Relatively quickly the partisanship that characterized the courts came to be tempered by professional standards that eschewed political associations and advocacy.

Even today, regardless of the charges hurled against the Supreme Court by both the Right and the Left, what critics call partisanship is actually deep and good-faith jurisprudential differences on both ends of the Court. This was also the case when, for a period of many decades, the Court had a liberal majority. And during that period — even during the years of the Warren Court in the 1950s and ’60s, when conservative precedents were overturned in large numbers and conservatives were often outraged — there were virtually no calls to pack or eliminate the Court.

During the confirmation hearings for Neil Gorsuch in 2017, I had an exchange with a Democratic senator who rattled off a series of 5–4 decisions to show that conservative justices were robotic partisans. I asked the senator if the four liberal justices showing the same consistency in dissent were also partisans. The reaction was disbelief. After all, the liberal justices were right in his eyes.

In reality, the attack on the Court as partisan is entirely disconnected from its actual voting record. It is a too-little-known fact that 44 percent of cases that come before the Supreme Court are decided unanimously. When you include nearly unanimous cases — those decided by 8–1 and 7–2 margins — that figure jumps to over 60 percent. It is also common for liberal and conservative justices to vote with colleagues on the opposite end of the ideological spectrum. In a case this year, for example, conservative Justices Thomas, Alito, and Kavanaugh joined liberal Justices Sotomayor and Jackson in the majority decision, while liberal Justice Kagan joined Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett in the dissent.

Liberal justices from Stephen Breyer to Elena Kagan have refuted claims that today’s Court is a partisan institution. Justice Kagan, as reported in Politico, spoke recently on this topic and “reject[ed] claims that the high court’s conservative majority is in President Donald Trump’s corner.” The fact is that the ongoing enthusiasm for packing or eliminating the Supreme Court is based less on the voting records and views of the justices than on the idea, as Senator Warren put it, that the Court should follow what she perceives as “widely held public opinion.”

For those on both ends of the political spectrum, judicial restraints on their favored policies can be frustrating or even infuriating. And sometimes, as history shows, the Court can get things wrong. On the other hand, those restraints often represent a firewall for natural rights.

Consider the attacks on free speech that came to a head during the Biden administration, when a coalition of forces in government, academia, and corporations created the largest censorship system in the history of our country. Free speech as guaranteed in the First Amendment has been understood throughout our history, almost universally among Americans, as a bedrock principle essential to all our rights. Yet there was an aggressive campaign between 2020 and 2024 to curtail free speech on the Internet and elsewhere by labeling it “disinformation,” “misinformation,” “malinformation,” or “hate speech.” Those standing in defense of free speech were dismissed, in the words of one law professor’s book, as members of a “cult of the Constitution.” This campaign followed a trend in Europe, where speech is increasingly criminalized. But European laws never understood free speech as a natural right, and Europe’s courts have never aggressively protected it.

Here in the U.S., on the other hand, one of the greatest triumphs for free speech came in the Supreme Court’s 2023 decision in 303 Creative LLC v. Elenis, which held that Lorie Smith, a Christian website designer, could refuse to provide services for a same-sex marriage. Justice Gorsuch, writing for the majority, argued that “the framers designed the Free Speech Clause of the First Amendment to protect the ‘freedom to think as you will and to speak as you think.’ . . . They did so because they saw the freedom of speech ‘both as an end and as a means’ . . . an end because the freedom to think and speak is among our inalienable human rights.”

Had 303 Creative been decided in a different way, states and cities could compel or curtail speech according to whatever their leaders viewed as discriminatory elements under public accommodations laws. Instead, the Court adopted a bright-line rule that business owners could decline to create expressive products from cakes to websites. The counter-majoritarian function of the Court worked in the 303 Creative decision to protect natural rights. Regardless of whether it reflected the will of the Colorado majority, it upheld the right of free speech.

We are living in a time of rage. It is not the first such time in our country. Indeed, America was born in rage. It was rage that fueled the Boston Tea Party. It was righteous rage, but rage all the same. It is especially during such periods that the judiciary must stand in defense of our individual natural rights. It is also especially during such times that we must stand as a people to prevent extremists of any ideological bent from politicizing or destroying our constitutional judicial system.

Ironically, those establishment figures trying to cancel the Court today are delusional in not foreseeing that they will be undermining their own freedom and security should they succeed. They might recall the answer of Abbé Emmanuel-Joseph Sieyès, often described as the Thomas Paine of the French Revolution, to the question of what he had done during the Revolution. “I survived,” he said.

The history of canceling courts is a history replete with unhappy endings. Courts are by necessity one of the first targets of revolutionaries. Following the October Revolution that brought the Bolsheviks to power in Russia, one of their first decrees was the “Abolition of Existing Legal Institutions.” Soon after came the establishment of the infamous People’s Courts. In revolution after revolution, newly-established courts carried out the purported will of the people with terrible consequences. In an age of rage, it is too often reason itself that is canceled.

Jonathan Turley is the J.B. and Maurice C. Shapiro Professor of Public Interest Law at George Washington University Law School. He received his B.A. from the University of Chicago and his J.D. from Northwestern University School of Law. He previously taught at Tulane University Law School. He has written for several publications, including The New York Times, USA Today, and The Wall Street Journal, and is the author of two books, The Indispensable Right: Free Speech in an Age of Rage and Rage and the Republic: The Unfinished Story of the American Revolution.
