news.title: Jelly Roll Under Fire After Leaked Video Shows Him Comparing Himself to Jeffrey Epstein in Bizarre Remark
news.text: Jelly Roll has been dragged into a bizarre online controversy involving Jeffrey Epstein after a short clip circulated appearing to connect the country star to the disgraced financier.The footage, discussed by commentator Nicole Arbour, opens with the question, 'How did Jeffrey Epstein happen?' before delivering a bizarre comparison involving Jelly Roll and fellow musician Ryan Upchurch.The remark has fuelled a fresh wave of criticism, although the available clip does not show Jelly Roll himself making the Epstein comparison. Instead, the controversy comes amid intense attention on the singer after he recently used a guest-hosting stint on Jimmy Kimmel Live! to take several pointed shots at Donald Trump.The Epstein Comparison Sparks Immediate BacklashThe controversy began with a brief clip in which Arbour made a provocative comparison involving Jelly Roll and Ryan Upchurch.'How did Jeffrey Epstein happen? With much work and help,' she said before adding, 'Just like Jeffrey Epstein, Ryan Upchurch has Jelly Rolled his wife to handle his dirty work.'The bizarre wording immediately created confusion over who was actually making the comparison and what exactly was being alleged.The supplied footage does not establish that Jelly Roll compared himself to Epstein, nor does it provide evidence connecting him to Epstein's crimes. The remark appears to come from the commentator discussing a separate dispute involving the musicians.That distinction has become important as the clip spreads online, where short videos can quickly lose their original context.Jelly Roll, whose real name is Jason DeFord, has recently been generating headlines for an entirely different reason after stepping in as guest host of Jimmy Kimmel Live!.Jelly Roll's Trump Jokes Put Him Back in the SpotlightJelly Roll pointed out that he had lost roughly 300 pounds and joked that he had effectively 'lost an entire Donald Trump'. He also referenced Trump's reported weight gain and his public history of making jokes about other people's appearances.The comments caught some viewers off guard because Jelly Roll's country music audience has sometimes assumed he was politically aligned with Republicans.During the programme, however, Jelly Roll made clear that he was not interested in fitting neatly into a political box.'If you wanted me to make jokes about Kamala Harris, you should have voted for her,' he joked.He later mocked the reaction from people threatening to stop listening to his music because of his comments, saying he would continue speaking his mind. His appearance therefore placed him firmly in the political conversation, even though he has previously described himself as having 'no political alliance'.His Past Makes the Backlash More ComplicatedJelly Roll's unusual public image has also played a major role in the attention surrounding him. The singer has openly discussed his past, including time spent in prison, drug dealing and struggles with addiction before transforming his life and building a successful music career.During his Kimmel appearance, he used that history to make fun of himself rather than presenting himself as a polished celebrity.'I don't even treat myself with reverence and dignity,' Jelly Roll joked, describing himself as a 'pastry' after looking in the mirror.However, the Epstein comparison is a different matter because Epstein's name carries an exceptionally dark association with sex trafficking and the exploitation of underage girls. Consequently, even an indirect or joking reference involving Epstein can trigger a powerful reaction online.

news.title: Dolly Parton brought divided Americans together. What can we learn from her? | Margaret Sullivan
news.text:
The moment that the world found out that Dolly Parton had died, I was in a hair salon in the reddest congressional district in New York state. The neighborhood on the shore of Lake Erie where I move every summer voted solidly for Donald Trump in 2024.

I often pass a lawn sign that has something misogynistic to say about New York’s Democratic governor, Kathy Hochul, and the mere mention of Kamala Harris’s name can bring derisive jokes. Of course, there certainly are liberals and independents to be found, but on balance the area leans right.

On my errands around town, I’ve heard scornful comments about transgender people, and the local Catholic church where I sometimes attend mass has a priest who, during a homily this summer, praised Trump for his war in Iran.

A lot of the people I’ve chatted with around town are outspoken about being anti-vaccine.

But when cellphones started pinging with the news about Dolly, it’s not overstating things to say that everybody was devastated. Stylists and customers alike seemed to feel a personal connection – to her music, to her philanthropy, to her sheer goodness.

How did Dolly, a rags-to-riches country music superstar with a Tennessee twang and bedazzled everything, manage to endear herself to Americans of every political stripe?

What was her secret – and does it hold some wisdom for the those who seek unity in this divided nation, who appreciate civility, who believe there’s an American ethos that transcends our ugly politics?

Some of it, surely, was that she had a gift for poking fun at herself, and joining in the laughter, as when she would say she didn’t mind being called a dumb blonde because she knew, after all, that she wasn’t dumb – and that she wasn’t a blonde. After her illness made headlines last year, she took to social media to make a simple point: “I ain’t dead yet.” She called herself a “Backwoods Barbie” in a song of that name.

Then there was her remarkable generosity. Her organization, Imagination Library, gave more than 330m books to children around the world. She founded it, in part, she said, because her father couldn’t read or write.

She never forgot where she came from, as she raised money for a new hospital in her home country in Tennessee, or offered $500 awards to local teenagers when they graduated from high school.

Still, how did she manage not to alienate the Maga world when she promoted the Covid-19 vaccine (the research for which she had helped fund)?

Again, the humor helped, as when she changed the words of one of her most famous songs, Jolene to something that rhymed, and sang “vaccine, vaccine” in promotional videos. You had to smile, and maybe decide to get the jab, or at least to tolerate those who did. And she never made it political.

“She practiced a unique brand of radical acceptance,” wrote Jad Abumrad in a New York Times essay this week. “No one would ever be thrown out of the Big Dolly Tent.”

And, though she is being mourned as something of an angel on earth, she was a razor-sharp businessperson. She was smart and savvy about it all, as befitted the superstar who chalked up 25 No 1 country singles over the years.

As Abumrad learned while interviewing and observing her at length as he created the podcast Dolly Parton’s America, she always told her own story.

“If a male talkshow host made a joke about her figure, she’d make an ever better joke about it. She was always two steps ahead of you. She never allowed herself to be a part of a story of which she was not the author.”

Can what Dolly Parton did be bottled somehow? Can her serendipitous mixture of humor, humility and humanity be sprinkled over our troubled waters to calm and soothe them?

Probably not – there is only one Dolly Parton – but that doesn’t mean we can’t learn something from this rare individual.

The rest of us might channel Dolly a bit more, and remember that a self-deprecating joke goes a long way toward easing tensions. We might recognize that financial success need not turn into ego glorification or arrogance.

And most of all, we might keep in mind that genuine generosity – if it comes from the heart – has the power to transcend politics.

Dolly Parton’s legacy, of course, resides in her wonderful songs, from Coat of Many Colors to 9 to 5. That’s what she would want.

But I don’t think she’d object if we also kept in mind her authentic kindness, her disarming wit – and the “radical acceptance” that fueled it all.

 Margaret Sullivan is a Guardian US columnist writing on media, politics and culture

news.title: Trump Drops Plans to Attend 25th Anniversary 9/11 Ceremony at Ground Zero
news.text:
Donald Trump is reportedly set to skip the Ground Zero commemorations in New York marking the 25th anniversary of the September 11, 2001 terrorist attacks.

The president, a New York native who built his real estate brand in the city, has been a familiar presence at 9/11 memorial events over the years.

But in 2026, he is expected to honor the victims for the second year in a row at a Pentagon remembrance ceremony after being denied a speaking role at the New York event, according to The New York Times.

Trump had sought to deliver remarks at the National September 11 Memorial and Museum, and his aides had reportedly conducted advance planning visits ahead of the anniversary.

Sources told the outlet that organizers at the museum are determined to keep the solemn ceremony free from partisan politics, noting that elected officials have not been permitted to speak there since 2012.

Vice President JD Vance is expected to attend the New York 9/11 memorial ceremony on behalf of the Trump administration, while former Presidents Bill Clinton, Barack Obama and George W. Bush are also anticipated to be there.

Trump is scheduled to return to Washington after attending the Republican Party’s midterm convention in Texas two days before September 11.

As he did the previous year, Trump is expected to speak at the Pentagon’s September 11 ceremony, where political leaders are still allowed to deliver addresses.

He will then leave the country for Ireland to visit his golf course where the Irish Open is being held.

His flight would be significantly easier on local air traffic going out of Joint Base Andrews in Maryland than from any of the New York-area airports. 

In a statement to the Times, White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly emphasized a remembrance of the victims but made no reference to the President’s specific plans. 

Our News Outlet has reached out to the White House for further comment. 

MORE STORY: Why America’s $40 Trillion Debt Won’t Trigger Fiscal Doom

The President also commemorated September 11 at the Pentagon last year, in a ceremony that was moved into the internal courtyard after the assassination of Charlie Kirk.

Trump pledged to always honor those who died on that day. 

‘We will defend the nation they served, the values they upheld and the freedom for which they died,’ he said. 

‘We will support our troops, we will protect our families, and we will preserve the American way of life for every future generation.

‘We will build taller, grow stronger, fight harder and soar higher, and together we will go forward as one people with one heart, one faith, one flag and one glorious destiny under almighty God,’ he added.

Trump did go to New York afterward, as he attended a Major League Baseball game between the New York Yankees and Detroit Tigers at Yankee Stadium. 

The last time Trump attended the Ground Zero ceremony was in 2024, when he was in the same company as Kamala Harris, as the two shared an awkward handshake. 

Trump and Harris appeared cordial at Ground Zero as they met for a second time in 24 hours following the first debate between the two, even sharing the handshake which was facilitated by Republican-turned-Democratic former New York City Mayor Michael Bloomberg.

Harris stood alongside President Joe Biden during the ceremony while Bloomberg acted as a buffer separating the current administration from Trump and his running mate Vance. Trump allegedly complimented Harris’s debate performance.

The attendance by Trump, Biden and Harris is rare and marks one of the few times the former president and current president have been in the same space.

The three would not be in the same space again until Trump’s second inauguration in Washington just four months later.

news.title: Top Newspapers Put Democrat Happy Talk on the Front Page
news.text:
So much of the “news product” we consume today isn’t about what has already happened. It’s about what could happen in the near future. Forget a microscope on the past. Get out the crystal ball. When it comes to the fortunes of the Democrats, the picture often takes on a rosy hue.

When conservatives dismiss our most “prestigious” newspapers as partisan Democrat rags, it comes from stories like the August 25 “News Analysis” editorial on the front page of The New York Times. It’s a piece by congressional reporter Carl Hulse titled "The Midterms Feel Like '06 Is Back Again." That’s a year when the Democrats gained 31 seats and Nancy Pelosi became Speaker of the House.

Twenty years later, Hulse insisted the GOP again faces “a grim backdrop” with “a steep challenge for Republicans.” Who would love a repeat of this scenario? Democrats. "It is striking," Sen. Charles Schumer of New York proclaimed in the Hulse piece. "The analogy is amazing." Rahm Emanuel, who headed the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee in 2006, added “This is 2006 2.0. The similarities are eerie.”

At the bottom of the column, they pushed more Happy News: “Path to Majority: An unpopular president has opened a door for Senate Democrats. See Page A-10.” The headline there: "Democrats Open More Paths To Win Back Senate Control."

Reporter Tim Balk proclaimed “Democrats have opened up more than one path to winning control of the Senate,” while acknowledging “Republicans still hold significant advantages.” Photographs implied momentum behind Sen. Jon Ossoff of Georgia, Mary Peltola in Alaska, Abdul el-Sayed in Michigan, and “centrist Democrat” Josh Turek in Iowa.

On August 26, the front page of The Washington Post carried more wishful imagination: “Canada trade fight could cost the GOP.” Reporters Gregory Schneider and Praveena Somasondarum relayed the obvious that an erupting trade war between the U.S. and Canada “added a new shock to midterm elections already dominated by price concerns.”

Inside the paper, the peppy headline was “Threat of higher prices over tariffs gives fresh life to Democratic arguments.” It sounds like cheerleading for inflation. The headline built off the article, with reporters oozing: “The threat of higher prices on consumer goods including gasoline, automobiles, and hockey sticks gave fresh life to Democratic arguments that Trump is destabilizing the economy.”

It’s certainly true that Trump’s aggressive tariff-tossing can build anxiety, which explains why his approval ratings are poor. The Iran war and the trade war aren’t reassuring to voters. But you can easily deduce that reporters are terrible at hiding their glee over the situation.

Trump campaigned on fighting inflation, the Post reporters wrote, “but since taking office last year has taken a series of actions widely seen as making things worse.” They touted Democrat victories in 2025 and polls showing disapproval of Trump on tariffs, and specifically on tariffs on Canadian goods.

The story ended with a Washington Post-Ipsos poll that found 43 percent of voters said they were “not as well off” as they were when Trump took office last January. That doesn’t look great. But at this point two years ago, the Washington Post poll had Kamala Harris up by four points…and in November, she lost the popular vote by 1.5 percent. 

Voters want a sense of the horse race, who might be winning and losing. But we’ve seen that polls can be wrong. We’ve certainly seen that liberal journalists habitually manufacture Keep Hope Alive content for Democrats. CNN segments on how Harris was going to turbo-charge “Brat Summer” memes for Gen Z and headlines like Time magazine’s “Don’t Underestimate Kamala Harris’ Good Vibes Only Campaign” didn’t actually work. They fizzled.

news.title: Trump to honor 9/11 at Pentagon after NYC memorial forbids speech: Report
news.text:
U.S. presidents and politicians who have given speeches on the Sept. 11 anniversary in years past have either done so at the Pentagon, from the White House, or in Shanksville, Pennsylvania, where the fourth plane crashed in 2001.

In 2025, President Trump spent the anniversary of the terrorist attack at the Pentagon ceremony, in which he both led a wreath-laying ceremony and delivered remarks reflecting on those who died and acted heroically during attack.

In 2024, then-Presidential candidate Trump attended the memorial ceremony at Ground Zero in Manhattan alongside then-Senator JD Vance, while former Vice President Kamala Harris attended the ceremony alongside then-President Joe Biden.

US OPPOSES 9/11 ATTACKERS’ SUPREME COURT BID TO AVOID DEATH PENALTY

Sept. 11, 2026 marks the 25th anniversary of the 2001 al-Qaeda terrorist attacks on the U.S. that killed 2,977 people in New York City, at the Pentagon, and in Shanksville, Pennsylvania. Two planes hit each of the World Trade Center buildings in lower Manhattan, while one plane hit the Pentagon. The plane that crashed in Shanksville was diverted from the terrorists’ suspected target of Washington, D.C., as patrons aboard the flight fought back against the al-Qaeda terrorists on the plane.

The Washington Examiner has reached out to the White House for comment on The New York Times report.

news.title: Democrats Try to Brush Aside 'Woke 1'
news.text:
"'Woke 1' was crazy." So said Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) on ABC News' "This Week" earlier this month. 

She said she was quoting New York City Councilman Chi Osse, whom The New York Times characterizes as "far left." This was where Ocasio-Cortez seemed to be located on the ideological spectrum after her surprise defeat of House Democratic leadership member Joseph Crowley in the 2018 Democratic primary. 

At that time, she was a 28-year-old former waitress and organizer for Sen. Bernie Sanders' (I-Vt.) 2016 presidential campaign. Today, a decade later, she's a nationally known figure often mentioned as a presidential candidate. In polls for the 2028 nomination, she ranks fourth in the RealClearPolitics average, behind 2024 nominee and former Vice President Kamala Harris, Gov. Gavin Newsom (D-Calif.), and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, and Polymarket places her odds of winning as better than any of theirs. 

As a possible national candidate, Ocasio-Cortez obviously has a motive to brush aside, as she did with a charmingly self-deprecatory laugh, the exotic positions she and other Democrats took on issues, particularly after the death of George Floyd in May 2020 and the ensuing multicity violent rioting. 

They included demands to "defund the police" or even abolish police departments, to step up the already institutionalized demands for "diversity, equity and inclusion" hiring, and promotions in bureaucracies, public and private, for racial reparations. These weren't just words: Cities such as New York, San Francisco, Chicago, and Minneapolis did hustle to partially defund their police departments. 

The Floyd riots and calls for defunding police were immediately followed by a sharp spike upward in violent crime. Liberals have characterized that spike as a response to COVID-19, but charts compiled by writer Steve Sailer make it clear that the spike began not with the lockdowns but with the riots and Woke 1 depolicing. 

At the same time, the lockdowns, enforced with Woke 1 censoriousness, were causing not just economic damage but also long-lasting harm to children who were kept out of teacher union-run schools long after it was clear children were not vectors of the virus. And Woke 1 transgender demands, for biological men on women's sports teams and public financing of even pre-adults' gender transition surgery, were advanced by the Biden administration and endorsed by Harris. 

Now there are numerous signs that the nation is putting Woke 1 so far in the rearview mirror as to be invisible and has little appetite for Woke 2. Items include: 

— The lack of visible vehement protests at the elimination of DEI programs, racial quotas and preferences, in federal regulations, in many state and local governments, and even in their strongholds in the universities. You hear grumbling about the Supreme Court's 2023 ruling in Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard, but nothing like the politically charged attacks on its 2022 overturning of Roe v. Wade. There's covert opposition and attempts to retain DEI under different labels, but you don't hear Democratic candidates talking about the issue. 

— Similarly, there's a dog-who-didn't-bark response to the Trump administration's effective shutdown of illegal immigration on the southern border. Missing from the political dialogue have been media stories about the asylum-seekers who are obliged now to pursue their claims not from somewhere in the continental United States but from a not particularly helpful or sympathetic Mexico or somewhere even more distant. 

— Violent crime rates seem sharply down. After the Floyd riots, homicides rose even more in 2021 and seemed on a trajectory to reverse all the enormous progress in crime reduction accomplished since the reforms pioneered by former Mayor Rudy Giuliani in New York in the 1990s. Homicides declined in 2025 to below the lowest numbers of the post-Giuliani years, and the FBI reported that violent crime dropped 9.3 percent, the biggest drop since 1936. For 2026, statistics aren't fully available, but there are starkly lower rates of violent crime in New York, and Baltimore has seen a huge drop in homicides in the 2020s. Why the huge drop in violent crime? No one is sure, but it comes as Democratic politicians are hastening to assure us that they never actually really wanted to abolish the police and the prisons when they were saying so back in Woke 1. 

— The revelations of the hypocrisy and lies of Dr. Anthony Fauci and other public health officials during the COVID-19 epidemic. Fauci, who, according to his diaries, delighted in partying with Washington elites, had to sit mute and invoke the Fifth Amendment as he was credibly attacked for having misled the public. Masking, he admitted privately, didn't prevent the spread of disease, even as he urged penalties for non-maskers. The vaccine, while reducing deaths, did not prevent transmission, as he had assured the nation. Fauci's efforts to discredit as "a conspiracy theory" the argument that the virus spread from a leak from the Wuhan laboratory he financed increasingly look very much like an effort to cover up the evidence that he financed the lab's gain-of-function research surreptitiously, to make the virus more dangerous, in violation of a presidential order. The initial order, by the way, came from former President Barack Obama, not President Donald Trump. 

Against this evidence of the discrediting of Woke 1, come recent victories and near victories of members of, or sympathizers with, the Democratic Socialists of America, whose platform calls for the abolition of police and prisons. Those candidates have been emphasizing economic issues, however, which pass muster in Democratic primaries but may not in general electorates in states such as Michigan. 

What is not apparent in the political landscape is nostalgia for Woke 1 police defunding, for heavy-handed statism like Fauci's COVID-19 regime, or for a revival of the Biden administration's open-borders immigration policy. Democrats may be able to capitalize on the current Trump slump this year. But for 2028, they may not be able to dismiss questions about Woke 1 and Woke 2 as flippantly as Ocasio-Cortez tried to do this month.

news.title: Trump plans to mark 9/11 at the Pentagon, not Ground Zero
news.text:
NEW YORK – President Donald Trump is not planning to attend a ceremony in New York for the 25th anniversary of the terrorist attack on the World Trade Center, in part because he wanted to deliver a speech and the annual event has long barred remarks, according to four people with knowledge of the events.

Trump’s team had conducted advance visits at the site and had initially signalled to officials in New York and in Washington that he intended to visit the memorial space known as Ground Zero, two of the people with knowledge of the events said.

The President’s interest in speaking on 9/11 was conveyed to memorial planners in recent weeks, three of the people with knowledge of the events said. But since 2012, politicians have been barred from speaking at the site.

The National September 11 Memorial & Museum, which oversees the site, has worked rigorously to keep the venue non-partisan and focused on the solemnity of the day.

Trump, a native New Yorker who talked often about the 9/11 attacks during his 2016 presidential campaign, is now expected to commemorate them at the Pentagon, two of the people with knowledge of the events said. The Pentagon also came under attack on 9/11.

Vice-President J.D. Vance is expected to represent the White House in New York.

The President will go to the Pentagon after he attends a mid-term political convention in Texas. Officials have discussed some kind of tribute to the terrorist attack victims during that convention, which takes place Sept 9 and 10.

There are other considerations that led to Trump honouring the day in Washington, including that he will depart the next day for his golf course in Doonbeg, Ireland, where the Irish Open tournament will take place.

Leaving from John F. Kennedy International Airport in New York City, or from Newark Liberty International Airport in New Jersey, would snarl air and motor traffic to a much greater extent than with Trump leaving from Joint Base Andrews in Maryland.

Trump last attended the ceremony at Ground Zero in 2024, when he stood alongside Vance, former mayor Michael Bloomberg, president Joe Biden and vice-president Kamala Harris.

None of the officials made formal remarks. Trump visited a fire station in New York City after the event.

The 2026 anniversary marks a quarter-century since the worst attack on the United States after the assault on Pearl Harbor.

Anna Kelly, a spokesperson for the White House, did not address the President’s plans in a response to an e-mail seeking comment.

“On the 25th anniversary of this tragic day, the President will remember those who were killed at the hands of evil terrorists, honour their loved ones, and pay tribute to the brave first responders who put their lives on the line to rescue their fellow Americans,” she said.

At the Pentagon, Trump will be allowed to speak, as he did in 2025 when he attended the remembrances there.

His speech that day came less than 24 hours after conservative activist Charlie Kirk, whose efforts to draw college-age voters into the MAGA movement were seen as significant to Trump’s 2024 victory, was shot and killed while speaking on a campus in Utah.

The ceremony had been intended to be held in a different spot that day but was moved to a new one amid security concerns about Trump after Kirk was assassinated.

“We recall the light of America’s best and bravest and the love that they showed in their final moments,” Trump said at the time.

“In their memory, we make a solemn pledge and a noble promise. We will honour always our great heroes, and you are our heroes.”

Trump has faced two assassination attempts and other murder-for-hire plots by alleged Iranian proxies. He has faced an uptick in threats since he began a war against Iran on Feb 28.

The 2026 event in Manhattan is expected to include former mayor Rudy Giuliani; former president Bill Clinton and his wife Hillary; former president George W. Bush and his wife Laura; and former president Barack Obama, among others, according to several people who have been close to the planning.

In the first decade after 9/11, elected officials would read poems and historic American documents, like the Gettysburg Address, at the ceremony.

But since 2012, the memorial has barred any speeches by politicians. Instead, politicians stand alongside their peers from opposing parties as families step onto a stage to read the names of the dead over the course of hours.

Trump’s advisers have discussed possibly taking federal control of the National September 11 Memorial & Museum, including as recently as in 2025. Families of the Sept 11 victims have in recent years criticised the site over its leadership and finances.

Trump, who was in New York on the day of the attacks, spoke to a New Jersey television station in the aftermath, saying that a building he owned had gained in stature because the twin towers had fallen.

That building, 40 Wall Street, “actually was the second tallest building in downtown Manhattan, and it was actually – before the World Trade Center – was the tallest”.

He went on: “And then, when they built the World Trade Center, it became known as the second tallest. And now it’s the tallest.” (The statement was not correct; 70 Pine Street, nearby, was taller than Trump’s building.) NYTIMES

His remarks come hours after Trump signed an executive order to change the name of Lake Ontario to “Lake America” amid the Trump administration’s escalating trade war with Canada.

news.text:

He argued that by pardoning Trump, Biden could deescalate tensions and break the cycle of partisan retribution.

A few days after Cox pitched the idea to Biden, Trump was indicted on state charges in Georgia over his alleged efforts to interfere in the presidential election in the Peach State. 

A presidential pardon would not have prevented prosecution in the Georgia or Manhattan cases. 

The federal cases against Trump, as well as the Georgia case, were dismissed after he defeated former Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election. 

Trump was convicted on 34 felony counts at the end of his Manhattan trial.

A few months before his conversation with Cox, Biden was asked by Fox News reporter Peter Doocy about potentially pardoning Trump.

Bis then added a sharply sarcastic aside: “A real profile in courage.”
